THE CONCEPT OF DIVINE REVELATION

WHAT THIS CHAPTER COVERS
- The concept of divine revelation.
- Its significance in Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
- Its impact on religious practice and on how religious texts are interpreted.
- The understanding of the transcendent in two traditions (Christianity and Islam).

KEY TERMS
- Transcendent: beyond normal or physical human experience. In religion, another word for God or the divine.
- Divine revelation: communication of knowledge about God by God.
- Universal revelation: God makes himself known to all people at all times in all places, e.g. through the beauty of creation and human goodness.
- Historical revelation: God reveals himself in a special way at a particular time and place - central to the three monotheistic faiths.
- Religions of the book: Judaism, Christianity and Islam - they believe God's revelation is contained in their scriptures.
- Five Pillars of Islam: profession of faith, prayer, fasting, almsgiving and pilgrimage.
- Incarnate: taking on human form.
- Mysticism: religious practice centred on knowing God through deep prayer, meditation and reflection - a personal journey to knowing God.
- Immanence: God being active and close in the world today and throughout history.

INTRODUCTION: ELIE WIESEL AND NIGHT
- Shows how our image of God is shaped by life experience. Adapted from Shannon Quigley's article 'Father and God (the Father) in Wiesel's Night as Response to the Holocaust'.
- Elie Wiesel: Romanian-born American writer, professor, political activist, Nobel laureate and Holocaust survivor; wrote fifty-seven books, including Night - semi-autobiographical, based on being a Jewish prisoner in Auschwitz and Buchenwald.
- The main character (Wiesel) is a very religious Jewish teenager: kosher food, classes on his faith, a bar mitzvah, weekly synagogue with his father.
- His mother and sisters are sent to the gas chambers; he clings to his father. 'All I could think of was not to lose him. Not to remain alone.' Holding hands recalls Shabbat walks to synagogue - reassurance and comfort.
- Father and son keep each other alive (train transport, snow as their only food, brutal inhumanity).
- At Auschwitz, men recite the mourner's Kaddish. Wiesel turns this prayer of praise into an accusation: 'The Almighty, the eternal and terrible Master of the Universe, chose to be silent. What was there to thank Him for?'
- The God of his childhood clashes with a God who seems absent; the darkness of night opposes the light of faith.
- Commentators suggest his relationship with his father may be a metaphor for his relationship with God.
- His father dies weeks before liberation; this and the horrors he sees cause him to lose faith.
- Low point: the slow hanging of a young boy (end of section four). Someone asks 'Where is God now?' and an inner voice answers: 'Where is He? Here He is - He is hanging here on this gallows ...' This can be read as God in solidarity with the suffering, or as the death of Wiesel's childhood faith and innocence.
- Years later, New York Times article 'A Prayer for the Days of Awe': 'Master of the Universe, let us make up ... Where were you, God of kindness, in Auschwitz? ... for the child in me, it is unbearable to be divorced from you for so long.'
- Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn: 'People found faith right there in the camp [and] they were strengthened by it.'

WHAT IS REVELATION?
- Chapter 6 explored concepts of God in myth, Hinduism, Shinto and the monotheistic religions. A transcendent God extends to the spiritual or unknowable dimension of reality.
- If God is unknowable, where do these understandings come from? Divine revelation - God reveals himself so people can know and understand him better.
- Christianity: the high point is Jesus Christ, Emmanuel ('God with us'), who became human to show us who God is.
- Islam: Allah is close through daily prayers and the words of the Qur'an. No one, not even the prophets, has seen God in this life; the mainstream view is believers will see him in the afterlife.
- God revealed himself to Moses in the burning bush (Exodus 3) - mosaic at St Catherine's monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai.
- Habakkuk 2:14: 'The earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.'
- Humans can never fully know God but can come closer. Revelation begins with God through human experience; humans choose whether to respond.
TWO FORMS OF REVELATION
- 1. Universal (general) revelation: God revealed to all people, all times, all places - through creation's wonder and beauty, the goodness and complexity of people, and all human experience. It gives rise to basic religious faith: a general belief in a transcendent being in the cosmos who loves and cares for humanity.
- 2. Particular, historical revelation: God reveals himself in a special way at a particular time and place. Central to the three Abrahamic faiths (Judaism, Christianity, Islam).

DIVINE REVELATION IN JUDAISM
- God revealed himself through Israel's turbulent history: the covenant with Noah after the Great Flood; the call of Abraham; the revelation of the mysterious name 'Yahweh'; the Exodus; the covenant on Mount Sinai.
- God always affirms: the Jews will always be his people and he their God.
- Revelation was first passed on orally, later written down as the Hebrew scriptures.
- The covenant relationship shapes every aspect of Jewish faith - prayer, worship, moral code. The covenant gives the laws recorded in the Hebrew scriptures. The Decalogue (Ten Commandments) contains key elements of the faith.
- God is 'A God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness'.
- Remembering God's saving presence at festivals like Passover shows how revelation affects practice.
- Revelation is central because the authority of the Bible, rabbinic tradition and Jewish law goes back to it - above all the giving of the Torah through Moses at Mount Sinai.
PROPHETS IN JUDAISM
- A prophet receives a revelation to proclaim to a larger community; so revelation and prophecy are intertwined in Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
- In Judaism Moses is the most important prophet. Hebrew word for prophet: navi - 'to proclaim, mention, call, summon'.
- Classical prophets: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi.
- Their messages: obey the law (ritual and moral); warnings about failing to keep the law; comfort after national catastrophes. Their written records became part of the Hebrew scriptures.
- Many prophets moved Judaism to a more clearly monotheistic faith, putting Yahweh at the centre of political, religious and cultural life.
- They reminded people of the Sinai covenant (worship only Yahweh, who chose Israel) and called them to live good and holy lives, be kind to the needy, be humble and work for peace and justice.

DIVINE REVELATION IN CHRISTIANITY
- Christians accept the Old Testament (Jewish Hebrew Bible or Tanakh) as central. Revelation began with creation and continued through the history of the Jewish people.
- Doug Hershey ('Is God Different in the Old and the New Testament?'): 'Both the Old and New Testaments reflect the same God ... God is Love in the Old Testament and God is Love in the New Testament.'
- Revelation unfolded over centuries; God communicated by words and deeds to build a personal relationship with all people.
- Jesus Christ is the high point of revelation; the gulf between God and humanity is bridged. His life, death and resurrection are the climax of God's involvement in history - God's most complete self-communication.
- Gaudium et Spes (Joy and Hope), Vatican II: 'The Lord Jesus Christ is the goal of human history ... the centre of the human race, the joy of every heart and the answer to all its yearnings.' (36)
- John 1:14: 'The Word became flesh and lived among us.' Jesus is the Word made Flesh, the definitive mediator between God and humanity.
- Key difference from Judaism: Jesus is the fullness of revelation.
- The Nicene Creed captures God's revelation culminating in sending his Son as saviour.
- Tradition and the authority of the Christian community guide interpretation. God is still revealing himself day by day (ongoing relationship); Christ will return in glory at the end of time; all that is needed for salvation is already revealed.
- Faith is needed to respond: a free, conscious, personal response to Jesus, celebrated in community (e.g. the Sacraments); necessary for salvation; ultimately a gift from God.

DIVINE REVELATION IN ISLAM
- Muslims believe God revealed himself to Abraham, Moses and the Hebrew prophets.
- They reject the divinity of Jesus but believe Jesus was God's greatest prophet (as stated in the textbook).
- Allah revealed himself for the last time in the seventh century - the complete and final guidance for humanity - contained in the Qur'an, the end of a long line of revelation. So the Qur'an is not open to change or criticism.
- The Qur'an not only reveals what God said but contains God's own words.
THE PROPHET MUHAMMAD
- The Qur'an was orally revealed to Muhammad, the final prophet. While meditating in a cave on Mount Hira he saw the archangel Gabriel (Jibril), who dictated Allah's messages.
- First words: 'Proclaim! In the name of thy Lord and Cherisher, who created - created man, out of a (mere) clot of congealed blood ... He who taught [the use of] the pen taught man that which he knew not.' (Qur'an 96:1-5)
- Popular view of the final words: 'This day I have perfected your religion for you ... and have chosen for you Islam as your religion.'
- Revealed bit by bit over about twenty-three years, beginning in Ramadan when Muhammad was forty, ending in 632 CE, the year of his death.
- Universal message: Allah is one, God of all, to be worshipped by all, the final judge.
- Muhammad is the Seal of the Prophets - the last prophet, so the Qur'an is the final revelation. The Qur'an is the eternal Word of God, treated with the greatest respect.
- The Qur'an describes Muhammad as of the highest moral excellence and a good example (Qur'an 68:4 and 33:21); it does not say he is God.
- Muslims try to live in the ways of the prophet; the Hadith (Prophetic sayings) are another key source of guidance.
- The Five Pillars are the practices through which Muslims offer themselves fully to Allah; unchanged for centuries, nothing to add or remove.
THE SHAHADA
- First Pillar: the profession of faith or 'bearing witness'. Two parts:
- 'ashhadum anna la ilaha illa 'l-Lah' - I bear witness that there is no god but Allah.
- 'wa anna Muhammadan rasulu 'l-Lah' - and I bear witness that Muhammad is the messenger of God.
- Jennifer Hitchcock ('The 5 Pillars of Islam'): the first half 'affirms Islam's absolute monotheism, an unshakable and uncompromising faith in the oneness or unity of God' and reliance on God; the second affirms Muhammad as messenger, last prophet and model for the community.
- Recommended as the first words to a newborn and last words to the dying; repeated at least twenty times daily; the basic part of the call to prayer.
- The 'heartbeat of Islam'; the most important pillar. Saying it with faith and conviction makes one a Muslim.

IMPACT OF REVELATION ON INTERPRETING TEXTS
- The three are religions of the book because of historical revelation recorded in sacred books.
- Judaism: God reveals himself generally in creation and experience, but the Hebrew scriptures are the most important source; they are the Word of God; law and festivals have a scriptural basis.
- Christianity: the Old and New Testaments are the basis of faith life - a source of consolation, challenge, inspiration and knowledge; reading and praying with the Bible helps people know Jesus. Distinctive: Jesus as the Word incarnate (John's Gospel) - the promise to God's chosen people fulfilled in the Incarnation.
- Pope Benedict (Deus Caritas Est, 1): 'Being a Christian is not the result of an ethical choice or a lofty idea, but the encounter with an event, a person, which gives a new horizon and a decisive direction.'
- Islam: the only source of knowledge of God is God, revealed in the Qur'an - literally God's work and his greatest gift. Hammudah 'Abd al-'Ati (Islam in Focus): the Qur'an 'originates life, quickens the soul, radiates guiding light'. Asma Afsaruddin: Islam's truth is anchored in scripture directly revealed by God and preserved in its original Arabic.

IMPACT OF REVELATION ON RELIGIOUS PRACTICE
- Religious practice includes worship services, religious clothing/symbols, prayer at set times, religious objects, dietary rules.
JUDAISM
- Monotheism (Deut 6:4-9; 11:13-21): the mezuzah - parchment in a decorative case with Torah verses of the Shema Yisrael ('Hear, O Israel, the Lord (is) our God, the Lord is One'). Recited daily by individuals and by the minyan (group of ten men) each morning; carried in phylacteries (small leather boxes) worn by men at prayer.
- Covenant relationship (Ex 3:8; Jer 7:23): Passover celebrates God's love and his bringing his people out of slavery to 'a land of milk and honey'; Moses led them and passed on God's laws.
- Belonging to God's people (Gen 21:4): circumcision on the eighth day after birth (the book says seven days here, but Gen 21:4 and the rest of the book say eight), by a trained mohel.
- God's greatness (Jer 10:6; Ps 96:4): the Kaddish, a thirteenth-century Aramaic prayer in every service, became the mourning prayer; it never mentions death but proclaims God's greatness.
CHRISTIANITY
- Monotheism (Mark 12:29; 1 Cor 8:6; James 2:19): Nicene Creed at the Eucharist - 'I believe in One God'.
- Jesus as Son of God (Luke 4:41; John 1:34): a Gospel reading in the ritual of each Sacrament.
- God as mystery (Matt 13:11; Eph 3:9): the Rosary - four sets of five mysteries: Joyful, Sorrowful, Glorious, Luminous. Rosary beads remind Catholics of God's providence.
- Trinity (Matt 28:19; 2 Cor 13:13): the sign of the cross - 'In the Name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit'.
ISLAM
- Monotheism (Suras 98, 110): the Shahada repeated many times daily.
- Muhammad as messenger (Sura 3:144; 47:2): Mecca, Muhammad's home town, is the focus of daily prayer and the Hajj; Hajj rituals recall Muhammad and Abraham; shows solidarity and submission.
- God as transcendent mystery (Sura 42:11): Allah is beyond understanding, so no images of Allah, Muhammad, or any human or animal figures in mosques - to avoid idolatry.

THE TRANSCENDENT IN TWO TRADITIONS
- Some realities are intangible - beyond material reality. The 'great intangibles': beauty, love, truth and goodness (e.g. powerful music, a parent's love, a sunset).
- A transcendent God is at the heart of all religions - the holy, separate from ordinary life yet giving it meaning.
- Tension between God as transcendent (beyond) and immanent (close and active in the world). God draws near yet can seem far away.
CHRISTIANS AND THE TRANSCENDENT
- Beauty, love, truth and goodness are the 'four footprints of God in the world' - evidence of God walking among us; they show God's closeness but also that he is unknowable.
- Tension between God as transcendent mystery and creator, and God as knowable through love, friendship and beauty.
- Pope Francis, Laudato si' (LS 12): St Francis saw nature as 'a magnificent book in which God speaks to us'; Wisdom 13:5 and Romans 1:20; Francis left part of the friary garden untouched for wildflowers so people could raise their minds to God; 'the world is a joyful mystery to be contemplated with gladness and praise.'
- The Incarnation: Jesus, Second Person of the Trinity, took flesh in the womb of the Virgin Mary; fully human and fully divine - two natures in one person, uniting God's immanence and transcendence. Jesus shows that God is Love.
- God's Spirit lives in the Christian community: 'Where two or three are gathered in my name' (Mt 18:20); 'By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another' (Jn 13:35).
- The Eucharist is the most radical breaking-through of the transcendent; for Catholics the 'source and summit' of Christian life (Catechism 1324).
MUSLIMS AND THE TRANSCENDENT
- God is the absolute other who communicates his will through Muhammad and the Qur'an.
- God's transcendence was a bulwark (barrier) against the polytheism around early Islam - absolutely non-negotiable.
- Jesus is honoured as a prophet but not the Son of God. The Trinity and Incarnation are rejected as reducing God's oneness and transcendence. Muhammad is never raised above prophet and holy man.
- Mary is recognised as the Mother of Jesus; a chapter of the Qur'an is devoted to her and Jesus' birth.
- Muslims can still feel drawn to this God everywhere and grow closer by following the Qur'an and Muhammad's guidance.
MYSTICISM
- Sufism: the mystical form of Islam - inward search for God, obedience to Islamic law, rejection of materialism; Sufis believe one can draw closer to God in this life. Whirling dervishes are a Sufi form of meditation.
- Rumi: thirteenth-century Iranian poet, son of a renowned Sufi scholar; his writings draw Muslims and non-Muslims to where the transcendent and immanent meet. Sufism has influenced Western spirituality.
- Christian mystics: Julian of Norwich, Meister Eckhart, St Teresa of Avila, St John of the Cross, St Hildegard of Bingen, St Francis of Assisi, Thomas Merton, Henri Nouwen, Thomas Keating.
- Both faiths: humans are not passive - the person can know, love and serve God.
CONCLUSION
- St Augustine of Hippo: 'Our hearts are restless until they rest in you, Oh Lord.' St Thomas Aquinas saw this restlessness for meaning as proof of God's existence.
- Islam: an innate desire for the transcendent; not praying is a sin against Allah and against human nature. Islam in Focus: 'It is an instinct of man to be inclined to worship great beings ... The Greatest Being and the Loftiest Goal of all is God.'
- Movement both ways: God reaching down (prophets, grace) and humans reaching up to know, love and serve him.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between universal and historical revelation.
rows.model_answer: Universal revelation is when God makes himself known to all people at all times and places, for example through the beauty of creation and the goodness of people; it gives rise to basic religious faith. Historical (particular) revelation is when God reveals himself in a special way at a particular time and place, such as to Moses at Mount Sinai. It is central to Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

rows.prompt: Explain how Elie Wiesel's image of God changed because of his experiences in the camps.
rows.model_answer: As a boy Wiesel had a strong Jewish faith in a God he hoped to obey. In the camps God seemed silent and absent, so he turned the Kaddish into an accusation. After watching a boy hanged and losing his father, he lost his faith. Years later he wrote of wanting to 'make up' with God, showing a longing for the God of his childhood.

rows.prompt: Name three moments in Jewish history when God revealed himself to the people.
rows.model_answer: God revealed himself in the covenant with Noah after the Great Flood and in the call of Abraham. He revealed the mysterious name 'Yahweh', and acted in the Exodus from Egypt. Above all he revealed himself in the covenant on Mount Sinai, where the Torah was given through Moses.

rows.prompt: Outline the role of the prophets in Judaism.
rows.model_answer: A prophet receives a revelation from God to proclaim to the community; in Judaism Moses is the most important. The prophets urged people to keep the law, warned them when they failed, and comforted them after disasters. They reminded people of the Sinai covenant to worship Yahweh alone and called them to be humble, kind to the needy and to work for peace and justice.

rows.prompt: Why is Jesus Christ so important to Christians in terms of revelation?
rows.model_answer: Christians believe Jesus is the high point and fullness of God's revelation, the Word made flesh (John 1:14). His life, death and resurrection are the climax of God's involvement in history, bridging the gap between God and humanity. Through knowing Jesus, Christians come to know that God is Love.

rows.prompt: Describe how the Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad.
rows.model_answer: While meditating in a cave on Mount Hira, Muhammad saw the archangel Gabriel (Jibril), who dictated Allah's messages, beginning 'Proclaim! In the name of thy Lord'. The Qur'an was revealed orally, bit by bit, over about twenty-three years, beginning in Ramadan when Muhammad was forty and ending in 632 CE, the year of his death.

rows.prompt: Why is the Shahada considered the most important Pillar of Islam?
rows.model_answer: The Shahada declares that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is his messenger. It affirms Islam's absolute monotheism and Muhammad as the final prophet. Accepting it means accepting the essence of the whole faith, and saying it with true conviction makes a person a Muslim. It is said to newborns and the dying and repeated at least twenty times a day.

rows.prompt: Give two examples of how divine revelation influences religious practice in Judaism.
rows.model_answer: Belief in one God (Deuteronomy 6:4-9) is expressed in the mezuzah, which holds the Shema, 'Hear, O Israel ... the Lord is One', recited daily. The covenant relationship is celebrated at Passover, remembering how God brought his chosen people out of slavery. Circumcision by a mohel seven days after birth is a sign of belonging to God's people.

rows.prompt: Describe the understanding of divine revelation found in two major world religions you have studied.
rows.model_answer:
Divine revelation is the communication of knowledge about God by God. In Judaism God revealed himself through Israel's history: the covenant with Noah, the call of Abraham, the revealing of the name 'Yahweh', the Exodus and the covenant at Mount Sinai. This revelation was first passed on orally and later written down as the Hebrew scriptures. The central act of revelation is the giving of the Torah through Moses, the most important prophet. The authority of the Bible and Jewish law comes from this. Prophets (navi) such as Amos and Micah called people back to the covenant to worship Yahweh alone. God is revealed as 'merciful and gracious, slow to anger'.

In Islam, Muslims believe God revealed himself to Abraham, Moses and the prophets, but that Allah revealed himself for the last time in the seventh century to Muhammad. In a cave on Mount Hira the archangel Gabriel dictated the Qur'an to him over about twenty-three years, ending in 632 CE. Muhammad is the Seal of the Prophets, so the Qur'an is the final, complete revelation. It contains God's own words, preserved in Arabic, and is not open to change. Muslims also follow the Hadith. The Shahada expresses this: no god but Allah, and Muhammad is his messenger.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. Two religions, about 10 marks each. May refer to: definition; universal vs historical revelation; Judaism - Noah, Abraham, Yahweh, Exodus, Sinai, Torah, oral then written, prophets, navi, covenant; Christianity - Old Testament, Jesus as fullness, Word made flesh, Gaudium et Spes, faith; Islam - Mount Hira, Gabriel, 23 years, 632 CE, Seal of the Prophets, Qur'an as God's words, Hadith, Shahada.

rows.prompt: Outline how two religious practices are influenced by the understanding of divine revelation found in one major world religion you have studied.
rows.model_answer:
In Christianity, God's revelation reaches its high point in Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh. Two practices show the impact of this revelation.

First, the sign of the cross. Through Jesus, Christians believe God has been revealed as a Trinity of three persons - Father, Son and Holy Spirit - in one God (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:13). This revealed belief is expressed each time Christians make the sign of the cross, 'In the Name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit', at the start and end of every prayer and during rituals. The Nicene Creed, recited at the Eucharist, also begins 'I believe in One God', expressing the revealed truth of monotheism.

Second, the Rosary. Christians believe God is a mystery revealed through Christ (Matthew 13:11; Ephesians 3:9). The Rosary, a Roman Catholic prayer, is centred on these mysteries, with four sets of five: the Joyful, Sorrowful, Glorious and Luminous Mysteries. By praying them, Catholics enter into the mystery of Christ's life, death and resurrection, and the rosary beads remind them of God's providence and care. In both practices, what Christians believe God has revealed shapes how they pray.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. Two practices from one religion, each linked clearly to a revealed belief (about 10 marks each). May refer to: Judaism - mezuzah/Shema, Passover, circumcision, Kaddish; Christianity - Creed, Gospel readings in Sacraments, Rosary, sign of the cross, Eucharist; Islam - Shahada, prayer facing Mecca, Hajj, no images in mosques. Scripture references credited.

rows.prompt: Outline the understanding of the transcendent in two religious traditions you have studied.
rows.model_answer:
The transcendent is what lies beyond normal human experience - in religion, God. There is a tension between God as transcendent (beyond us) and immanent (close and active in the world).

Christians believe they can explore the mystery of God through the 'great intangibles' of beauty, love, truth and goodness, called the 'four footprints of God in the world'. These show God's closeness yet also that he is beyond us. Pope Francis in Laudato si' says nature is 'a magnificent book in which God speaks to us'. Above all, in the Incarnation, Jesus became fully human while remaining fully divine, uniting God's immanence and transcendence. God is present in the community ('Where two or three are gathered', Mt 18:20) and most radically in the Eucharist, the 'source and summit' of Christian life. Mystics like Julian of Norwich and St Teresa of Avila sought God through deep prayer.

In Islam, God is the absolute other who communicates his will through Muhammad and the Qur'an. His transcendence was a bulwark against the polytheism of the time and is non-negotiable. Jesus is honoured as a prophet, but the Trinity and Incarnation are rejected as reducing God's oneness. No images of Allah are allowed. Yet Muslims can draw close through the Qur'an and Muhammad's guidance, and Sufi mystics like Rumi seek God in this life.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. Two traditions, about 10 marks each. May refer to: definition; transcendence vs immanence; Christianity - four footprints, Laudato si', Incarnation, two natures, community, Eucharist, Christian mystics; Islam - absolute other, Qur'an, bulwark against polytheism, rejection of Trinity/Incarnation, no images, Mary honoured, Sufism, Rumi; Augustine's restless heart.

rows.prompt: Using the example of Elie Wiesel, explain how a person's image of God can be influenced by their life experiences.
rows.model_answer:
Elie Wiesel was a Romanian-born American writer, Nobel laureate and Holocaust survivor whose book Night is based on his time in Auschwitz and Buchenwald. As a boy he had a traditional Jewish upbringing: kosher food, a bar mitzvah and weekly synagogue with his father. His image of God was of a God to be studied and obeyed.

In the camps his mother and sisters were killed and he clung to his father. When the men recited the Kaddish, he turned it into an accusation: God 'chose to be silent. What was there to thank Him for?' The God of his childhood now seemed absent. Watching a young boy hanged, he heard a voice say 'Here He is - He is hanging here on this gallows', which can mean the death of his childhood faith or God suffering with the victims. When his father died weeks before liberation, he lost his faith. Yet years later he wrote, 'Master of the Universe, let us make up', showing that his experiences changed but did not end his search for God.
